title: Backtesting and live signals with ai
author: danni3boi
selftext: Just curious if others have had a similar experience. I’m giving ai a clear written set of rules for entries and exits. I’m using frontier lvl ai to process my requests. It does it python writing and backtests and spits out results. Results look off from my experience, say I told it to backtest the last few days and I know mentally what kind of trades were available. I tell it to give me a list of all the entries and exits it took. Import it into my charting and it’s just wrong. Missed tons of entries in the rules set, enters in 80% of the rules but not following the 20% matters, a lot. I’ve gone so far as making a shared charting platform where I mark out where signals should have been so it can learn how within the rule set my entries and exits make sense. Rerun tell it to analyze it just still can not do it. I gave up after a week of trying this. Any insights would be appreciated.

comments.author: Outrageous_Band9708
comments.body:
AI LLM are not deterministic.

they cannot be the gate behind which you make decisions

sure it may work today and this week 5 times.

but wht bout 2 months from now when the model got updated and it doesn't use the exact same rules for things?

you are asking for trouble by using an AI as the gate

.

replies.author: Vegetable-Rub-8241
replies.body: completely agree, and I'd go further: the gate should never be an LLM at all, not today's version and not a future one. use the model to draft ideas or write code, then let a fixed deterministic evaluator, unrelated to any LLM, decide pass or fail on data it never saw. that way a model update upstream can't quietly change what counts as a good result downstream.

replies.author: Outrageous_Band9708
replies.body: yes, use ai to write deterministic gates in code. that code can be used reliably

comments.author: Vegetable-Rub-8241
comments.body: this is the actual failure mode, not the one people usually warn about. an LLM writing python to simulate your own rules is asking a language model to be a deterministic executor, and that's not what it's good at, it'll follow 80% of a rule set and quietly drop the exact clause that matters. the fix isn't a better prompt, it's separating the two jobs: let the model help you turn your rules into code, then run the actual backtest and grading with a deterministic engine that either matches your rule or it doesn't, no interpretation. did you ever try having it just generate the rule as strict code instead of asking it to execute the logic itself each time?

replies.author: danni3boi
replies.body: I didn’t I’ll try this next. Just tell it to make a python backtest script strictly based on my rule set and run the backtest manually.

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body: You hit the exact problem most people miss. An LLM is a language model, not a deterministic executor - it'll follow 80% of your rules and silently ignore the clause that actually filters out bad trades. The fix isn't better prompting, it's separating the jobs. Use the AI to draft ideas and write code, then run that code through a fixed deterministic evaluator on data it never saw during development. That's why tools like trademates.co exist - they grade strategies on unseen data to catch curve fitting before you lose money. Your instinct to mark signals on a shared chart is solid, but you need a system that doesn't rely on the LLM being the gatekeeper.

comments.author: hakobpapazian
comments.body:
The 20% it's missing is the useful signal here, not the bug. When you execute those rules yourself, you're filling gaps with judgment you never actually wrote down. "Rejection off the level," "clean structure," whatever it is, you resolve it in your head instantly and don't notice you did. The AI can only run what's literally on the page, so the trades it skips are precisely the ones where your unwritten judgment was carrying the entry.

That's why marking the missed entries and telling it to "learn" doesn't work. There's no rule there to learn, there's a pattern in your head that hasn't been converted to a condition yet. You're asking it to infer an unstated rule from examples, which frontier models are bad at in a way that looks like stupidity but is really underspecification.

Two ways to use this. If you want the backtest to match you, take ten of the missed entries and force yourself to write the exact condition that made them valid, in terms a stranger could check without seeing the chart. That process usually surfaces one or two rules you didn't know you had. If you can't articulate the condition even to yourself, that's the more important finding: part of your edge is discretionary and can't be automated as-is, which means a mechanical backtest will always understate it and you shouldn't trust the AI's numbers as your real performance.

Quick check to confirm it's underspecification and not a code bug: take a single missed entry, hand the AI just that bar and your rules, and ask which specific rule permits or blocks entry there. It'll usually tell you plainly that nothing in the ruleset triggered, which points at the gap rather than the execution.
